items.title: Operational observable model of the force branch: parameters, preparations, observation times, readout, units and additive error
items.statement:
## Definition

Fix a force model of the force branch [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: a
nondegenerate open time window $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, an open configuration
domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ for $N\ge1$ particle labels, with the
collision set removed when the model's force law is singular there
([[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a)), fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), and a force map
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$$
with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz hypotheses of clause
(iii) of that postulate. Fix one inertial frame of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]) and read all times and positions
below in this frame; dimensions and units are those of [[def-cm01-units]].

**Protocol.** An **operational observable model** of this force model in the
frame consists of the following data.

1. **Parameters.** A nonempty set $\Theta$, the **model parameters**, with a
   family $(F_{\theta})_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of force maps on
   $I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$, each satisfying the standing
   hypotheses of the force branch, so that $\bigl(I_{0},Q,(m_{i}),F_{\theta}\bigr)$
   is a force model of that branch for every $\theta\in\Theta$.
2. **Preparations.** A nonempty set $Z$, the **apparatus and preparation
   settings**, and a map $\zeta:Z\to I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$,
   written $\zeta(z)=\bigl(t_{0}(z),x_{0}(z),v_{0}(z)\bigr)$, assigning to
   each setting an initial datum of the model.
3. **Observation times.** A finite strictly increasing family
   $t_{1}<\dots<t_{k}$ in $I_{0}$ with $k\ge1$, the **observation times**.
4. **Definedness.** For every $(\theta,z)\in\Theta\times Z$ the model with
   force map $F_{\theta}$ and initial datum $\zeta(z)$ has a unique maximal
   motion $x_{\theta,z}:J_{\theta,z}\to Q$, with $J_{\theta,z}\subseteq
   I_{0}$ an open interval containing $t_{0}(z)$
   ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]], [[pthm-cm02-ivp]]), and the protocol requires
   $[t_{1},t_{k}]\subseteq J_{\theta,z}$. Its **state** at $t_{j}$ is
   $$s_{\theta,z}(t_{j}):=\bigl(x_{\theta,z}(t_{j}),\,w_{\theta,z}(t_{j})\bigr) \in Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N},$$
   where $w_{\theta,z}:=x_{\theta,z}'$ is the coordinate velocity.
5. **Readout.** An integer $d\ge1$ and a map
   $$R:\Theta\times Z\times\bigl(\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N}\bigr)^{k} \longrightarrow\mathbb R^{d},$$
   the **readout**, whose value at $(\theta,z)$ is the tuple of the $k$
   states of clause 4 in order; the **prediction map** is
   $$\Phi:\Theta\times Z\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{d},\qquad \Phi(\theta,z):=R\bigl(\theta,z,s_{\theta,z}(t_{1}),\dots, s_{\theta,z}(t_{k})\bigr).$$
   No regularity of $R$ in the parameters is assumed; continuity,
   differentiability or measurability in $\theta$ or in the states is an
   additional hypothesis, declared where it is used.
6. **Units.** For each $j\le d$ a dimension $[\Phi_{j}]$ from
   [[def-cm01-units]] is declared, and the coordinate $\Phi_{j}(\theta,z)$ is
   read in the corresponding unit.
7. **Error and observation.** A probability space $(\Omega,\mathfrak F,
   \mathbb P)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]), an open **error domain**
   $V\subseteq\mathbb R^{d}$ with $0\in V$, and a random element
   $\varepsilon:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{d}$ with $\varepsilon(\omega)\in V$ for
   every $\omega$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]). The
   **observation** at $(\theta,z)$ is the random element
   $$Y_{\theta,z}:=\Phi(\theta,z)+\varepsilon:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{d},$$
   the sum being read coefficientwise in the declared units, so that the
   coordinate $\varepsilon_{j}$ carries the dimension $[\Phi_{j}]$ for every
   $j$ (rule (b) of [[def-cm01-units]]).

### Well-definedness and conventions

**Well-definedness.** The prediction map is well defined: for each
$(\theta,z)$ the maximal motion is unique by [[pthm-cm02-ivp]], and clause 4
puts the observation times in its interval. For fixed $(\theta,z)$ the
observation is a random element in the sense of
[[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]: the map
$\tau(u):=\Phi(\theta,z)+u$ is a translate of $\mathbb R^{d}$, hence
continuous, its preimages of Borel sets are Borel, and
$Y_{\theta,z}^{-1}(B)=\varepsilon^{-1}\bigl(\tau^{-1}(B)\bigr)\in\mathfrak F$
by the measurability of $\varepsilon$. This repeats the argument of
[[def-cm-measurement-model]] for the additive-error observation model with
$h=\Phi$; the mathematical interface used below is exactly that definition.

**No hypothesis on the error is part of the definition.** Mean zero,
square-integrability, boundedness, a stated law, independence across
repetitions, stationarity and calibration are **not** part of the definition;
each must be stated at its point of use, with its exact quantifiers, exactly
as in [[def-cm-measurement-model]]. In particular a deterministic error, for
which $\varepsilon$ is a constant random element, is admitted; the definition
then records a modelled residual rather than a probabilistic error.

**Frame relativity of the protocol.** The observation times are times of the
declared frame, and the prediction map is read in that frame's coordinates;
a change of inertial frame changes the coordinate times and the readout of
the same physical protocol. The framework therefore always names the frame
in which a protocol is specified; no frame-independent reading of $\Phi$ or
$\varepsilon$ is asserted.

**Scope.** The definition constructs an interface, not a measurement. It does
not assert that any apparatus realizes the protocol, that any preparation can
be reproduced, that the declared error domain or law is correct, or that
$\Phi$ agrees with any physical system. A statement that a physical procedure
satisfies the protocol requires separate empirical evidence, and no such
evidence is part of this item.
items.strategy: Definition with explicit well-definedness and convention paragraphs; no proof supplied.

K. K. items.title: Calibration of a mechanical apparatus against the primitive standards of the framework: reference inputs, deviations, rules and calibrated prediction maps
items.statement:
## Definition

Fix the force branch and one inertial frame as in
[[def-cm18-observable-model]], and fix the observation times and readout of a
protocol of that definition. A **calibration family** is a family
$$\bigl(\Phi_{c}\bigr)_{c\in C},\qquad \Phi_{c}:\Theta\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{d},$$
of prediction maps on a nonempty parameter set $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$,
$p\ge1$, in declared numerical coordinates, indexed by a
nonempty set $C$ of **apparatus settings**, each $\Phi_{c}$ arising as the
prediction map of an operational observable model of the force branch as in
[[def-cm18-observable-model]]; the setting $c$ selects the apparatus state in
which the readout is taken. The dimensions and units are those of
[[def-cm01-units]]. Coordinate $\theta_j$ is the numerical coefficient of a
quantity in one fixed unit $u_j$ with declared dimension; different coordinates
may use different units. Choose positive numerical scales $s_j$ and define
$\|v\|_s=(\sum_j(v_j/s_j)^2)^{1/2}$. This norm compares normalized
numerical deviations, not sums of different physical dimensions.

A **calibration datum** for this family consists of:

1. a finite family $\bigl(\theta^{(1)},\dots,\theta^{(n)}\bigr)$, $n\ge1$, of
   **reference inputs** $\theta^{(r)}\in\Theta$, together with a **reference
   realization** of each: the parameter value $\theta^{(r)}$ is fixed by
   declared realizations of the primitive quantities of the framework — a
   duration in seconds, a length in metres or a mass in kilograms
   ([[def-cm01-units]], [[post-cm01-spacetime]], [[post-cm01-worldlines]]
   clause (v)) — supplied by a **reference standard** under stated
   conditions;
2. for each $r$ a declared **deviation** of the reference input from its
   nominal value $\theta^{(r)}_{\mathrm{ref}}$ assigned by the standard:
   either a bound $\|\theta^{(r)}-\theta^{(r)}_{\mathrm{ref}}\|_s\le\delta_r$
   for a declared dimensionless number $\delta_r\ge0$, or a
   Borel random element $\eta_r:\Omega\to\mathbb R^p$ of numerical deviations with a stated law
   on a stated probability space ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]),
   so that the reference input is the random value
   $\theta^{(r)}_{\mathrm{ref}}+\eta_r(\omega)\in\Theta$ for every $\omega$;
   every addition is coordinatewise in the fixed unit $u_j$, and the
   deviations are not required to belong to $\Theta$;
3. a set $Y\subseteq(\mathbb R^{d})^{n}$ of admissible **reference
   observations** and a declared vector $y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{n})\in Y$;
4. a **calibration rule**, that is, a map
   $$\Gamma:D\longrightarrow C,\qquad (y,\theta_{\mathrm{ref}})\longmapsto c,\qquad D\subseteq Y\times\Theta^n .$$
   Here $\theta_{\mathrm{ref}}=(\theta^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ref}},\ldots,\theta^{(n)}_{\mathrm{ref}})\in\Theta^n$
   and $(y,\theta_{\mathrm{ref}})\in D$; each observation coordinate is read
   in the fixed readout unit of [[def-cm18-observable-model]].

Given the datum, the **calibrated setting** is $c:=\Gamma(y,\theta_{\mathrm{ref}})$ and the
**calibrated prediction map** is $\Phi_{c}$. This is the physical instance of
the calibration structure of [[def-cm-calibration-rule]], with the framework's primitive quantities as reference
realizations. If normalized coordinates $\vartheta_j=\theta_j/s_j$ are
used, the deviation norm is exactly the Euclidean norm of that mathematical
structure. A rule with fixed references is only a slice of this two-input
rule, not a rule that discards reference values.

### Well-definedness and conventions

The sets $\Theta$, $C$, $Y$, the maps $\zeta$, $R$ of the underlying
protocols, the reference inputs, the deviations and the rule $\Gamma$ are
data. Nothing in the definition requires $\Gamma$ to be injective,
continuous or measurable, or to return a setting whose prediction map is
accurate; [[def-cm-calibration-rule]] records the same conventions for the
mathematical structure. The deviation clauses 2 are the only interface
through which the reference standard's uncertainty enters, and they must be
carried into every quantitative conclusion about $\Phi_{c}$; a calibration
from which the deviations have been dropped supports no quantitative
statement.

Calibration is the step at which the framework's units and a standard's
values assign numerical values to model parameters. The framework by itself
fixes no numerical value of any parameter (clause (e) of
[[def-cm01-units]]), and the value $\theta^{(r)}_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the value
attached by the standard, not a measured value of this item. A calibrated
prediction map is a model object; a claim that an apparatus realizes it
requires separate evidence.

items.title: Repeated-observation protocols of the force branch: adopted IID and second-moment sampling hypotheses and the sample mean
items.statement:
## Definition

Fix an operational observable model of the force branch
([[def-cm18-observable-model]]) in a fixed inertial frame, with parameter set
$\Theta$, preparation settings $Z$, prediction map $\Phi:\Theta\times Z\to
\mathbb R$, probability space $(\Omega,\mathfrak F,\mathbb P)$, error domain
$V\subseteq\mathbb R$ and error random element $\varepsilon$; the readout is
scalar here ($d=1$), since the mathematical sampling interface used below is
stated for real random variables, and vector readouts are treated
coordinatewise where needed.

A **repeated-observation protocol** for this model consists of

1. a **repetition count** $n\ge1$ and one error random element
   $\varepsilon_{k}:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ for each $k=1,\dots,n$, with
   $\varepsilon_{k}(\omega)\in V$ for every $\omega$, the error of the $k$-th
   repetition on the common probability space
   ([[def-probability-measure]],
   [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]);
2. the **observations** $Y_{k}:=\Phi(\theta,z)+\varepsilon_{k}$ at a fixed
   pair $(\theta,z)\in\Theta\times Z$: the same parameter value and the same
   preparation are declared for every repetition, so that the repetition
   changes only the error.

The protocol **satisfies the IID sampling hypothesis** when the family
$(\varepsilon_{1},\dots,\varepsilon_{n})$ — equivalently the family
$(Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n})$ — is independent and identically distributed in the
sense of [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]; it
**satisfies the second-moment hypothesis** when $E\bigl[Y_{1}^{2}\bigr]<+\infty$.
Under both hypotheses the common mean and variance
$$\mu:=E[Y_{1}]\in\mathbb R,\qquad\sigma^{2}:=\operatorname{Var}(Y_{1})\in[0,+\infty)$$
are defined by [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]], the **sample mean** is
$$\overline Y:=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^{n}Y_{k},$$
and the mathematical consequences of the two hypotheses are those of the
sampling model [[def-cm-iid-sampling-model]], namely the conclusions of
[[lem-cm-finite-iid-sample-mean-bound]]: $E\bigl\lvert\overline Y-\mu\bigr\rvert^{2}
=\sigma^{2}/n$ and, for every $a>0$,
$$\mathbb P\bigl(\bigl\lvert\overline Y-\mu\bigr\rvert\ge a\bigr) \le\frac{\sigma^{2}}{n\,a^{2}}.$$

### Well-definedness and conventions

The IID and second-moment hypotheses are **adopted model hypotheses about the
repetitions**, not consequences of the protocol and not properties of the
data. Independence of the errors fails when successive repetitions share a
systematic effect, when the apparatus drifts between repetitions or when the
same recorded data are reused; identical distribution fails when the
preparation or the conditions change between repetitions. A use of the
displayed bounds must state both hypotheses, the declared law (if any) of
$\varepsilon$, and the conditions under which the repetitions are claimed to
be comparable.

The sample mean $\overline Y$ is a random variable of the model. The
definition attaches no observed value to $\mu$ or $\sigma^{2}$; in
particular $\sigma^{2}$ is model data and not a measured uncertainty, as
[[rem-cm-inference-and-uncertainty-scope]] records for the mathematical
interface. A physical claim that a stated procedure satisfies the IID
sampling hypothesis requires separate empirical evidence and is not part of
this item.

items.title: Model testing for the force branch: what a test specifies, what rejection and retention establish, and what is not claimed
items.statement:
## The ingredients a test must specify

A test of a null set is a rejection region $R$ inside a measurable data space
$S$ for a specified family $(\mathbb P_{\theta})_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of
probability measures and a specified null set $\Theta_{0}\subseteq\Theta$;
its power function is $\beta(\theta)=\mathbb P_{\theta}(R)$ and its size is
$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_{0}}\beta(\theta)$
([[def-cm-statistical-test-and-size]]). The size is computed from the null
set and the family alone; no alternative set and no prior distribution enter
it, and a test at level $\alpha$ rejects a true null with probability at most
$\alpha$ **under the specified family**.

For the force branch of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]], a family and a
rejection region are obtained only after specifying: one inertial frame; an
operational observable model of [[def-cm18-observable-model]] — parameters,
preparations, observation times, readout and units — whose prediction map is
computed from the maximal motions supplied by [[pthm-cm02-ivp]]; a
calibration datum of [[def-cm18-calibration]] with its reference deviations;
a sampling model of [[def-cm18-sampling-model]] with its adopted IID and
second-moment hypotheses, or an explicitly different dependence model; the
law of the error random element, or its declared bounds; a null set
$\Theta_{0}$ of parameter values; and a rejection region. Until these data
are fixed, the phrase "a test of Newton's law" names no test, and the size
and power of no test are defined.

## What rejection and retention establish

A rejection is a decision about the specified triple of null family,
apparatus behaviour and sampling assumptions. It is evidence against that
triple at the declared size; it is not a proof that a force law, a spacetime,
or classical mechanics is false, and the realized discrepancy does not by
itself identify which ingredient failed. A discrepancy may expose the force
law, a wrong or incomplete calibration, a changed preparation, correlated
errors violating the sampling hypothesis, or an analysis error; separating
these requires further stated models and further data. Conversely, retaining
the null is not proof of the null: a test with low power fails to reject
alternatives it cannot distinguish, and the absence of a rejection under one
rejection region carries no information about the size of an effect.

The indices of this page attach no probability to a parameter value. The
level of a confidence set is a pre-data infimum of coverage probabilities
([[def-cm-confidence-set-and-coverage]]); a likelihood value is the density
of the observed datum at a parameter value, not the probability of the value
([[def-cm-likelihood-function]]); and a size is a supremum over the null set
of probabilities of a region. In particular a $p$-value computed from a
specified family is not the probability that the tested hypothesis is true,
as [[rem-cm-inference-and-uncertainty-scope]] records for this mathematical
interface. The cited interpretive warnings of the sources state the same
properties for statistical tests in general.

## What agreement does not establish

Agreement of a prediction with observations is evidence for the combined
adopted assumptions — force model, calibration, preparation, sampling model
and analysis — at the stated uncertainty; it is not a deductive proof of the
model and it does not test "classical physics" as a whole, only the specified
family. A finite sample can fail to exhibit a feature that the declared
sampling model predicts with positive probability per trial; such a sample is
not by itself a refutation of the model, and the elementary probability of
that outcome under the sampling model is part of the specification, not an
empirical result.

No datum, no rejection, no retention, no $p$-value, no effect size and no
measured uncertainty is asserted anywhere in this item.
items.strategy: Scope and status remark; no proof supplied.

items.title: Numerical error in a prediction pipeline: certified velocity-Verlet bounds, additive per-step error, the analytic long-time branch, and the separation from model error
items.statement:
## Model error and numerical error are different

The prediction map of an operational observable model
([[def-cm18-observable-model]]) is defined from the exact maximal motions of
the force model. A numerical pipeline replaces those motions by a computed
sequence, and at least five distinct errors must be kept apart: the
**model-versus-nature error**, the difference between the model's exact
motion and a physical system, about which the framework proves nothing; the
**discretization error**, the difference between the computed sequence and
the exact flow of the same model; the **implementation error**, the per-step
residual of the arithmetic actually performed; the **observation error**
$\varepsilon$ of the protocol; and the **sampling error** of a repeated
protocol. Only the second and third admit the certified statements below,
and those statements are always about the model.

## Finite-time discretization error of velocity Verlet

Fix a splitting $H=A+B$ of a mechanical Hamiltonian and the velocity-Verlet
map $V_{h}=K_{h/2}\circ D_{h}\circ K_{h/2}$ of
[[def-cm-splitting-hamiltonian-and-verlet-map]], and let $\Phi_{t}$ be the
exact flow of the system ([[def-cm-local-flow-of-an-autonomous-system]]).
Under the hypotheses of [[thm-cm-verlet-finite-time-error-is-quadratic]] — a
bounded convex tube with the local truncation constants $h_{1},C_{1}$ of
[[lem-cm-verlet-local-truncation-error-is-cubic]], a compact set $K_{1}$
inside the tube, a step $0<\lvert h\rvert\le h_{1}$ and $n\lvert h\rvert\le
T$, with the computed iterates $z_{j}=V_{h}^{j}(z_{0})$ and the exact flow
points $y_{j}=\Phi_{jh}(z_{0})$ both retained in $K_{1}$ — the finite-time
bound
$$\lVert z_{n}-y_{n}\rVert\le C_{1}h^{2}\frac{e^{LT}-1}{L}\quad(L>0), \qquad \lVert z_{n}-y_{n}\rVert\le C_{1}Th^{2}\quad(L=0)$$
holds with $L$ the sup-norm bound on the derivative of the Hamiltonian
field over the tube. The hypothesis that the iterates remain in the compact
set is part of the statement; no first-exit claim is made here.

## Additive per-step error

The implementation error is not analysed as floating-point arithmetic.
Instead, [[lem-cm-roundoff-accumulation-in-one-step-schemes]] assumes
computed points $x_{j}$ with $\lVert x_{j+1}-V_{h}(x_{j})\rVert\le\eta$ and a
Lipschitz bound for $V_{h}$ with constant $1+Lh$, and concludes
$$\lVert x_{n}-z_{n}\rVert\le\eta\,\frac{(1+Lh)^{n}-1}{Lh} \le\eta\,e^{LT}\frac{T}{h}\quad(nh\le T,\ L>0),$$
and, for any observable $F$ Lipschitz with constant $\Lambda$,
$\lvert F(x_{n})-F(z_{n})\rvert\le\Lambda\eta\bigl((1+Lh)^{n}-1\bigr)/(Lh)$.
A Lipschitz readout of the protocol therefore converts a trajectory bound
into a bound on the difference of the computed and exact prediction maps by
multiplication with its Lipschitz constant. The number $\eta$ is a
**hypothesis on the per-step residual**, not a measurement of an arithmetic
unit, and the lemma says nothing about the distribution of rounding.

## The analytic long-time branch

For analytic splitting data on a complex neighbourhood, with the domain
radius, step-size restriction $0<h\le h_{0}$ and compact retention of the
iterates through the stated time window, there are constants $C,c>0$ with
$$|H_{h}(z_{n})-H_{h}(z_{0})|\le Cnh\,e^{-c/h},\qquad |H(z_{n})-H(z_{0})|\le Ch^{2}\quad\text{when }nh\le e^{c/(2h)},$$
where $H_{h}$ is the finite optimally truncated modified Hamiltonian of
[[thm-cm-analytic-verlet-energy-on-exponential-times]]. Adding the
implementation error, [[lem-cm-separate-roundoff-energy-accumulation]] gives
$$|H(x_{n})-H(x_{0})|\le 2C_{E}h^{2}+Cnh\,e^{-c/h}+C_{G}n\eta$$
for computed points with per-step residual at most $\eta$. Both statements
keep every hypothesis of the cited items, including the small-step bound,
the holomorphy domain and the retention of iterates in the compact set; the
first is a discrete-time energy estimate, not an estimate of the original
trajectory on exponentially long times.

## What is and is not certified

The bounds above compare the computed sequence with the exact motion of the
same model. They are silent about the difference between the model and a
physical system, and they do not certify any apparatus. Exact
symplecticity of the Verlet map is a statement about exact arithmetic
([[rem-cm-scope-of-the-certified-verlet-estimates]]); the additive residual
hypothesis is the only interface through which the arithmetic enters, and
rounded symplecticity is not claimed. Consequently a numerically computed
trajectory, fit or error budget is a computation on the model under the
stated hypotheses, not an experiment, not a measurement, and not evidence
for the model. The constants $C_{1},L,h_{1},C,C_{E},C_{G},c$ are data of
the cited statements; no numerical value of any of them for a physical
system is asserted here.

items.title: The Galilean regime of the framework: frame-relative protocols, the absence of an intrinsic slow-motion parameter, and the empirical status of a validity claim
items.statement:
## The adopted kinematic regime

The spacetime of the framework is the affine event space with its surjective
absolute-time covector, its three-dimensional Euclidean spatial displacement
space and its fixed orientation ([[post-cm01-spacetime]]); it contains no
inner product on the full displacement space, no light cones, no null
displacements and no universal speed bound. The frames are the adapted
affine charts of these data, and the allowed changes between them are the
Galilean transformations $t'=t+b$, $x'=Rx+vt+a$ with $R\in SO(3)$
([[post-cm01-frames]]); the resulting kinematic laws, the
frame-independence of vanishing coordinate acceleration and the group
structure of the changes are the content of
[[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]]. The force model transforms by its own
declared covariance rule ([[post-cm02-force-superposition]]), and the
existence and uniqueness statements for maximal motions are stated in the
chosen frame ([[pthm-cm02-ivp]]).

## Protocols are frame-relative

An operational observable model ([[def-cm18-observable-model]]) is specified
in one inertial frame: its observation times are times of that frame, its
readout is a function of the coordinate states, and its error random element
carries the units of the readout coordinates. Changing the frame shifts the
coordinate times, transforms positions affinely and rotates and boosts
coordinate velocities, so the same physical protocol has a different
prediction map in a different frame. A measurement model must therefore name
its frame, and a claim that two frames "agree" is a claim about the declared
transformation law of the model, not a separate empirical discovery.

## No intrinsic slow-motion parameter

The dimension group of the framework is generated by length, duration and
mass ([[def-cm01-units]] clause (a)); the framework contains no quantity of
dimension $\ell\tau^{-1}$ that is a constant of nature. Consequently the
framework cannot by itself form a dimensionless parameter that measures how
close a system is to some other kinematic regime, and it states no numerical
cutoff: every regime statement such as "the motion is adequately described
by this model at the required accuracy" is an **external, empirically
qualified premise** of a use of the model, not a theorem of it. Quantifying
the error of such a statement would require a distinct model carrying a
speed scale together with a limit or approximation theorem relating the two
models; no such theorem is asserted, used or presupposed here.

## What is not claimed

The framework distinguishes no inertial frame ([[rem-cm01-model-limit]]);
"at rest" is a frame-relative description, not an absolute state. No
measured speed, no numerical validity boundary, no comparison with any other
kinematic framework, and no claim that a physical system is exactly
Galilean is made. The Galilean transformations are exact symmetries of the
adopted model by [[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]]; whether a physical
situation is adequately represented by the model is an empirical question
that this item leaves open.

items.title: The electromagnetic bridge: what a charged-particle coupling must add to the framework, what the force branch then yields, and what is not imported
items.statement:
## What the framework already supplies

The particle side of the framework is complete on its own terms: labels with
$C^{2}$ worldlines parametrized by frame time and fixed positive masses
([[post-cm01-worldlines]]); a force branch in which the force map is declared
model input with standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz hypotheses
([[post-cm02-force-superposition]]); motions, unique maximal motions and the
continuation criterion ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]], [[pthm-cm02-ivp]],
[[pthm-cm02-continuation]]); the mechanical quantities and their balance
theorems, conditional on the declared interaction structure
([[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]], [[pthm-cm03-frame-transformations]],
[[rem-cm03-conservation-scope]]); and the operational observable model
through which predictions at observation times are read
([[def-cm18-observable-model]]). The framework contains no charge, no field
and no coupling law.

## What an electromagnetic coupling must add

A charged-particle coupling is a **new physical assumption**, not a
consequence of the framework, and it must supply at least:

1. **Charge attributes.** To each label an attribute with a declared
   dimension and unit. The dimension group of the framework is generated by
   length, duration and mass alone ([[def-cm01-units]] clause (a)); the
   dimension and unit of charge, and of the components of any field used,
   must therefore be declared by the coupling and cannot be inferred from
   this framework.
2. **Field maps.** Electric and magnetic fields (or the corresponding
   potentials) as maps with declared domains, regularity, sources and
   boundary or radiation conditions, supplied by an independently developed
   electromagnetic model; the particle framework constrains none of these.
3. **A coupling law.** An added force map $F^{\mathrm{EM}}$ per label, for
   instance a declared function of the fields, the charge and the label's
   velocity in the chosen frame, as in the Lorentz force of the cited
   electromagnetic treatment. The coupling law is adopted: the framework
   neither derives it nor tests it.
4. **Field-side bookkeeping.** If statements about the energy or momentum of
   the combined system are wanted, the field contributions and their balance
   with the particles must be declared as separate objects; this framework
   contains no field energy or field momentum.

## What the force branch yields conditionally

Once a coupling has been declared, the mechanical theorems apply to the
total force map $F+F^{\mathrm{EM}}$ provided it satisfies the standing
hypotheses of the force branch (continuity and state-local Lipschitz,
locally uniformly in time) on the declared domain: then
[[pthm-cm02-ivp]] and [[pthm-cm02-continuation]] give the local, unique and
maximal motions of the coupled model, and the balance laws of the
[[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta|balance page]] apply with the coupling
force among the external contributions.

No field-momentum theorem is imported. With the electromagnetic force
treated as external to the declared particle labels, the particle mechanical
momentum alone need not be conserved; the balance laws record the exchange
through the external force, and the open-system boundary of
[[rem-cm02-open-system-warning]] applies. A conservation statement for
matter plus field requires the field contributions of item 4 above as
additional declared data, and is not a consequence of this framework.

## What is not claimed

No field equation, no value or dimension of any charge or coupling constant,
no derivation or validation of a coupling law, no prediction of any
electromagnetic phenomenon and no measured electromagnetic quantity is
asserted. The observable models of [[def-cm18-observable-model]] acquire an
electromagnetic readout only after a coupling has been declared; until then
this framework is silent about electric and magnetic effects.

items.title: The quantum bridge: a distinct framework, the shape of a quantization or correspondence result, and the absence of any such theorem in this framework
items.statement:
## Two distinct frameworks

This framework describes a physical system by labels with $C^{2}$ worldlines
parametrized by frame time, fixed masses ([[post-cm01-worldlines]]) and a
declared force map whose maximal motions are deterministic objects
([[post-cm02-force-superposition]], [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]],
[[pthm-cm02-ivp]]). The point-particle idealization itself is an adopted
description: the cited treatment records that it neglects the
quantum-mechanical uncertainties of the position. A quantum framework is a
**different model** with its own primitives — states, observables and
probability postulates — and none of its objects is defined here. The
probability space of an operational observable model
([[def-cm18-observable-model]]) is attached to the declared error random
element of a coordinate readout; it is not a state, not an observable
algebra, and not a probability rule for a physical system, as
[[rem-cm-inference-and-uncertainty-scope]] already records for the
mathematical interface.

## What a correspondence result would require

Relating the two frameworks is a mathematical task with two parts:

1. a **reconstruction or quantization construction**: a declared map from
   data of the mechanical model to the objects of the quantum framework, with
   its domain, its algebraic consistency conditions and its treatment of
   ordering ambiguities. The cited treatment presents canonical quantization
   as exactly such a prescription between Poisson brackets and commutators;
   it is an additional rule, not a theorem of this framework, and the
   replacement of a classical phase-space variable by an operator is not a
   deduction inside it.
2. **limit theorems with explicit hypotheses**: statements that specified
   quantum predictions converge, in a stated topology and under stated
   regularity and small-parameter conditions, to specified classical
   predictions, with an error estimate. The cited treatment performs the
   classical limit only under an explicit inequality on the phase of the
   wavefunction and obtains the Hamilton-Jacobi equation at leading order;
   that is an approximation argument with hypotheses, not an identity
   between the two frameworks.

## What is not claimed

No quantization construction, no semiclassical limit theorem, no
correspondence principle, no derivation of quantum mechanics from this
framework and no derivation of this framework from a quantum one is
asserted. No quantum phenomenon is predicted, explained or excluded here;
no trajectory is assigned to a particle between preparations and detections
of a quantum experiment; and the error random element of an observable
model is not identified with a quantum measurement outcome. A bridge
between the frameworks would be a separate development stating its own
construction, hypotheses and error control, and would not change the status
of any statement on this page.

items.title: Contract for a future reported experiment of the framework: source, setup, calibration, procedure, sampling, observations, uncertainty and interpretation
items.statement:
## What a reported experiment must supply

A later **experiment item** for this framework is a report of an actual
measurement, and must be assembled from an actually retrieved primary source
and record, separately:

1. **Source.** A primary report with a resolvable reference, read in full:
   an apparatus paper, an instrument report or a data release, not a
   textbook exposition of a law and not a secondary anecdote.
2. **Setup.** The prepared system in the vocabulary of the model: labels,
   declared parameters, configurations and the initial-data region
   ([[def-cm18-observable-model]]); the apparatus and its settings; and the
   **calibration** with its reference inputs and their declared deviations
   ([[def-cm18-calibration]]).
3. **Procedure.** The measurement protocol in a declared inertial frame:
   observation times, readout, units; the **sampling model** with its
   adopted IID and second-moment hypotheses, or an explicit statement of the
   dependence or drift that replaces them ([[def-cm18-sampling-model]]); and
   the selection of the reported data.
4. **Observations.** The values actually reported by the source, with their
   units and their conditions, quoted or transcribed faithfully. If the
   source records no quantitative detail, only a correspondingly limited
   qualitative account is supported; no precision, count or value may be
   supplied from elsewhere.
5. **Uncertainty.** The statistical and systematic uncertainty treatment of
   the source and of the calibration: Type A evaluation from repeated
   observations, Type B evaluation from declared bounds and reference data,
   combination and expansion, and the deviations of the reference standards.
   Measured inputs of the comparison model carry their uncertainties and
   conditions into the conclusion ([[rem-cm-inference-and-uncertainty-scope]]).
6. **Interpretation.** A specified comparison between the reported
   observations and a specified prediction of the model, including the
   idealizations the prediction uses; a specified discrepancy measure; and a
   specified test — data space, model family, null set and rejection region
   with its size ([[def-cm-statistical-test-and-size]]) — or a specified
   estimation or confidence construction ([[def-cm-confidence-set-and-coverage]],
   [[def-cm-likelihood-function]]). Agreement is evidence for the joint
   assumptions of model, apparatus and analysis, and a discrepancy may
   expose any of them.

## What is and is not available now

The treatments cited by this framework are model exposition; they are not
primary reports of a measurement of the framework's parameters under a
controlled preparation, and the citations of this page therefore close no
experiment obligation. No experiment item, no observation, no measured
value, no uncertainty, no $p$-value and no effect size is asserted by this
page. The worked computations on the companion page are **proposals**: they
compute what a protocol would imply under declared hypothetical data and
uncertainties. Turning such a proposal into a reported experiment requires
all six items above, in particular an actually retrieved primary source.

title: Measurement, uncertainty and later bridges — Examples

items.title: A proposed small-angle pendulum calibration of a gravitational parameter: linearized propagation and a bounded nonlinearity remainder on declared data
items.statement:
## Example

Adopt as the declared physical content of a **proposed protocol** the ideal
planar pendulum of the cited treatments: parameters $m,l,g>0$, exact
equation $ml^{2}\theta''+mgl\sin\theta=0$, and small-angle idealization
$T=2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$ for the period $T$ of a small oscillation, whose
linearization at $\theta=0$ is the quadratic mode of angular frequency
$\omega=\sqrt{g/l}$. The model and its small-angle idealization are **declared
data** of the example, adopted from the cited treatments; the exact
finite-amplitude period discrepancy is not derived here. No measurement is
performed and no measured value is used.

**The declared protocol.** The protocol of [[def-cm18-observable-model]]
reads two coordinates of one oscillation: the pendulum length $l$ and the
period $T$, both with the dimensions and units of [[def-cm01-units]]
($[l]=\ell$, $[T]=\tau$). As its prediction map for a gravitational
parameter it uses
$$h:U\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad U:=\bigl\{(l,T)\in\mathbb R^{2}:l>0,\ T>0\bigr\},\qquad h(l,T):=\frac{4\pi^{2}l}{T^{2}},$$
an idealization whose exact justification would require the small-angle
period relation of the cited treatments. The difference between the exact
period of the ideal pendulum at finite amplitude and $2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$ is a
**model discrepancy** of the protocol, denoted $\delta\ge0$ in units of
$\tau$; this example neither estimates nor bounds $\delta$, and a
quantitative use of the protocol must supply it separately. The reference
deviations of any calibration of the apparatus are likewise data of
[[def-cm18-calibration]] and are not part of the computation below. A
calibration setting has the explicit form $c=\Gamma(y,\theta_{\mathrm{ref}})$
in fixed parameter units; the proposal supplies no reference observations
or realized setting. In the calculations below $l$ and $T$ denote numerical
coefficients in metres and seconds and $h$ the numerical coefficient in
metres per second squared. Euclidean norms are applied to these fixed
numerical coordinates, not to sums of physical quantities of different
dimensions; their constants depend on this coordinate convention.

**Declared data.** Fix a nominal input $\mu=(l_{0},T_{0})\in U$ with
$l_{0},T_{0}>0$ and radii $0<\rho_{l}<l_{0}$, $0<\rho_{T}<T_{0}$, and put
$$U_{B}:=(l_{0}-\rho_{l},\,l_{0}+\rho_{l})\times(T_{0}-\rho_{T},\,T_{0}+\rho_{T}) \subseteq U,$$
an open convex box. Let $X=(l,T):\Omega\to U_{B}$ be a square-integrable
random vector with
$$E[X]=\mu,\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(X)=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{l}^{2}&\sigma_{lT}\\ \sigma_{lT}&\sigma_{T}^{2}\end{pmatrix}.$$
All entries are declared **model data**: no reading of an apparatus is
asserted. With $h$ as above:

1. $h$ is $C^{\infty}$ on $U$, with
   $$\frac{\partial h}{\partial l}(l,T)=\frac{4\pi^{2}}{T^{2}}=\frac{h(l,T)}{l}, \qquad \frac{\partial h}{\partial T}(l,T)=-\frac{8\pi^{2}l}{T^{3}} =-\frac{2h(l,T)}{T},$$
   so $Dh(\mu)$ has the two components $h(\mu)/l_{0}$ and $-2h(\mu)/T_{0}$;
2. the Hessian on $U$ is
   $$H_{h}(l,T)=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\dfrac{8\pi^{2}}{T^{3}}\\[2mm] -\dfrac{8\pi^{2}}{T^{3}}&\dfrac{24\pi^{2}l}{T^{4}}\end{pmatrix},$$
   and on $U_{B}$ its operator norm is at most the Frobenius bound
   $$B:=\Bigl(2\Bigl(\frac{8\pi^{2}}{(T_{0}-\rho_{T})^{3}}\Bigr)^{2} +\Bigl(\frac{24\pi^{2}(l_{0}+\rho_{l})}{(T_{0}-\rho_{T})^{4}}\Bigr)^{2} \Bigr)^{1/2};$$
3. the covariance of the linearization
   $T_{\mu}(x)=h(\mu)+Dh(\mu)\cdot(x-\mu)$ is the $1\times1$ matrix
   $$\operatorname{Cov}\bigl(T_{\mu}(X)\bigr) =\frac{16\pi^{4}}{T_{0}^{4}}\,\sigma_{l}^{2} -\frac{64\pi^{4}l_{0}}{T_{0}^{5}}\,\sigma_{lT} +\frac{64\pi^{4}l_{0}^{2}}{T_{0}^{6}}\,\sigma_{T}^{2},$$
   which for uncorrelated inputs ($\sigma_{lT}=0$) reads
   $$\operatorname{Cov}\bigl(T_{\mu}(X)\bigr) =\frac{16\pi^{4}}{T_0^4}\Bigl(\sigma_{l}^{2}+\frac{4l_{0}^{2}}{T_{0}^{2}}\,\sigma_{T}^{2}\Bigr) =h(\mu)^{2}\Bigl(\frac{\sigma_{l}^{2}}{l_{0}^{2}} +\frac{4\sigma_{T}^{2}}{T_{0}^{2}}\Bigr);$$
4. for the nonlinearity remainder
   $R:=h(X)-h(\mu)-Dh(\mu)\cdot(X-\mu)$ one has the pointwise bound
   $\lvert R\rvert\le\frac{B}{2}\lvert X-\mu\rvert^{2}$, hence
   $\lvert E[R]\rvert\le E\lvert R\rvert\le\frac{B}{2}E\lvert X-\mu\rvert^{2}$,
   and if $E\lvert X-\mu\rvert^{4}<+\infty$ then
   $E[R^{2}]\le\frac{B^{2}}{4}E\lvert X-\mu\rvert^{4}$.

Since $E[X]=\mu$ gives $E\bigl[Dh(\mu)(X-\mu)\bigr]=0$, the mean of the
reading $\hat g:=h(X)$ satisfies
$\bigl\lvert E[\hat g]-h(\mu)\bigr\rvert\le\frac{B}{2}E\lvert X-\mu\rvert^{2}$,
while the exact variance of the linearization is the matrix of clause 3. The
actual variance has the explicit correction of
[[cor-cm-linearization-error-bounds]]: with $s^2=\operatorname{Var}(T_\mu(X))$
and $M_4=E|X-\mu|^4$,
$$|\operatorname{Var}(\hat g)-s^2|\le B\sqrt{s^2M_4}+\frac{B^2}{4}M_4.$$
The box ensures $M_4\le(\rho_l^2+\rho_T^2)^2<\infty$; the model discrepancy
$\delta$ and the reference deviations of the calibration contribute further
unquantified terms. The protocol is a proposal: no value of $l$, $T$, $g$,
$\sigma_{l}$, $\sigma_{T}$, $\sigma_{lT}$, $\delta$ or $B$ is a measurement
here.

items.title: Repeated observation of a uniform motion: prediction map, adopted IID sampling hypotheses and the resulting sample-mean bound on declared data
items.statement:
## Example

**The declared model.** In the force branch [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]
take $N=1$ label of mass $m>0$, time window $I_{0}=\mathbb R$, configuration
domain $Q=\mathbb R^{3}$ and the **zero force map** $F(t,x,v):=0$. It is
continuous and state-Lipschitz with constant $0$, so it satisfies the
standing hypotheses of the branch. With $e_{1}$ the first standard basis
vector and a parameter $v\in\mathbb R$ of dimension $\ell\tau^{-1}$
([[def-cm01-units]]), declare the initial datum $\zeta(v):=(0,0,v e_{1})$ at
time $t_{0}=0$, so that $\Theta:=\mathbb R$ and the datum map $\zeta$ of
[[def-cm18-observable-model]] is defined. Fix an observation time $t_{1}>0$
and the **position readout** $\Phi(v):=x_{v}(t_{1})\cdot e_{1}$, where
$x_{v}$ is the motion of the model with datum $\zeta(v)$; the readout has
dimension $\ell$ and is read in metres.

**The motion.** The curve $x_{v}(t):=(vt,0,0)$, $t\in\mathbb R$, is a
motion of the declared model with datum $\zeta(v)$: its coordinate velocity
is $w_{v}(t)=(v,0,0)$ ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]), its coordinate
acceleration vanishes, and $m\ddot x_{v}=0=F$ identically
([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]). Hence the prediction map is
$\Phi(v)=v\,t_{1}$, of dimension $\ell$ with $[t_{1}]=\tau$.

**The repeated protocol.** Fix $n\ge1$ and adopt the IID sampling hypothesis
and the second-moment hypothesis of [[def-cm18-sampling-model]] for the
errors $\varepsilon_{1},\dots,\varepsilon_{n}$ of $n$ repetitions of the
protocol at the same parameter $v$ and the same preparation, on a common
probability space. Suppose additionally that $E[\varepsilon_{1}]=0$ and
$\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_{1})=\sigma^{2}\in[0,+\infty)$; these two
statements are extra model hypotheses, not part of either definition. Then
the observations are $Y_{k}=v t_{1}+\varepsilon_{k}$ and
$$\mu:=E[Y_{1}]=v\,t_{1},\qquad \sigma^{2}=\operatorname{Var}(Y_{1}),\qquad \overline Y=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^{n}Y_{k}.$$
Consequently, by [[lem-cm-finite-iid-sample-mean-bound]],
$$E\bigl\lvert\overline Y-v t_{1}\bigr\rvert^{2}=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{n}, \qquad \mathbb P\bigl(\bigl\lvert\overline Y-v t_{1}\bigr\rvert\ge a\bigr) \le\frac{\sigma^{2}}{n\,a^{2}}\quad(a>0).$$

**A declared illustration.** With the declared model data
$v:=2\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$, $t_{1}:=3\,\mathrm s$, $\sigma^{2}:=4\,\mathrm m^{2}$
and $n:=16$, the nominal prediction is $v t_{1}=6\,\mathrm m$ and the bound
reads $\mathbb P(\lvert\overline Y-6\,\mathrm m\rvert\ge1\,\mathrm m)\le\frac{4}{16\cdot1}=\frac14$.
These numbers are hypothetical illustration of the formula; they are not
measured values, and no apparatus is asserted to realize the protocol.

D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 printing), Section 1.2, printed pages 2-5 (PDF pages 8-11): Newton's second law for a particle and the free particle with constant velocity

items.title: Frame change of a declared protocol: how the prediction map and an additive error transform between two inertial frames
items.statement:
## Example

Fix the force branch and a model as in [[def-cm18-observable-model]], and fix
two inertial frames $F$, $F'$ of the model with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$
and $(t',x')$. By [[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]] there are $b\in\mathbb R$,
$a_{0},v\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and $R\in SO(3)$ with
$$t'(p)=t(p)+b,\qquad x'(p)=R\,x(p)+v\,t(p)+a_{0}\qquad\text{for every event }p .$$

**The protocol in $F$.** Take a protocol of [[def-cm18-observable-model]]
with a single observation time $t_{1}\in I_{0}$ and the **position readout**
$\Phi(\theta,z):=x_{\theta,z}(t_{1})\in\mathbb R^{3}$ of dimension $\ell$,
read in metres ([[def-cm01-units]]); the observation is
$$Y=\Phi(\theta,z)+\varepsilon$$
for an error random element $\varepsilon:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3}$ on a
probability space $(\Omega,\mathfrak F,\mathbb P)$.

**The protocol in $F'$.** The same event at which the readout is taken has
$F'$-time $t_{1}+b$; reading the same label position in $F'$ at that time
defines the prediction map of the protocol in $F'$,
$$\Phi'(\theta,z):=x'_{\theta,z}(t_{1}+b)=R\,\Phi(\theta,z)+v\,t_{1}+a_{0},$$
and the $F'$-coordinates of the recorded point are
$$Y':=R\,Y+v\,t_{1}+a_{0}=\Phi'(\theta,z)+R\,\varepsilon,$$
so the additive-error form is preserved with the rotated error
$\varepsilon':=R\varepsilon$.

**Transform of the error law.** Suppose $\varepsilon$ is square-integrable
with mean $E[\varepsilon]=0$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$ in the sense of
[[def-cm-covariance-matrix-of-a-random-vector]]. Then $\varepsilon'=R\varepsilon$
has mean $0$ and covariance
$$\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon')=R\,\Sigma\,R^{\mathsf T},$$
and $\lvert\varepsilon'\rvert=\lvert\varepsilon\rvert$ componentwise in the
Euclidean norm because $R$ is orthogonal. In particular an additive error
declared in one frame is **not** an additive error with the same law in
another: the law transforms by the pushforward under $R$, and the prediction
map acquires the known affine term $v\,t_{1}+a_{0}$. A protocol must declare
the frame of its readout and of its error model.

references.title: D. Tong, Dynamics and Relativity (Cambridge lecture notes, Lent 2013), Section 1.2.1, printed page 5 (PDF page 11): the Galilean transformations t' = t + b, x' = Rx + vt + a between inertial frames

K. K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Part CM: Classical Mechanics (title page last edited September 1, 2026), Section 1.1 point (v), chapter pages 2-3 (PDF pages 6-7): the transfer of the radius vector and of velocity and acceleration between frames, with the warning that rotating frames require more care

JCGM 100:2008, Evaluation of measurement data - Guide to the expression of uncertainty in measurement (BIPM, 2008 corrected version), clauses 5.1.2 and 5.2.2, equations (10) and (13): propagation of covariance through a linear relation, used here for the rotating error

items.title: A finite sample can miss a predicted outcome with positive probability: an elementary product-model counterexample
items.statement:
## Statement refuted

Let a repeated-observation protocol of [[def-cm18-sampling-model]] satisfy
its IID sampling hypothesis and its second-moment hypothesis, and let $A$ be
an event of a single observation with $0<\mathbb P(A)=p<1$. Then **every
finite sample $(Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n})$ of the protocol contains at least one
outcome in $A$** for every $n\ge1$; equivalently, if a finite sample
contains no outcome in $A$, the declared sampling model is refuted.

references.title: S. Greenland, S. J. Senn, K. J. Rothman, J. B. Carlin, C. Poole, S. N. Goodman and D. G. Altman, Statistical tests, P values, confidence intervals, and power: a guide to misinterpretations, European Journal of Epidemiology 31 (2016), 337-350, sections on absence of evidence and on the interpretation of non-significant results
Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Section 2.1 on independence and Section 2.2.1 on i.i.d. sequences and their finite product laws
NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, section 7.1.3.5, 'What are Type I and Type II errors?', on failing to reject a hypothesis and the meaning of false negatives

items.physical_scope: A counterexample to a stated inference rule for finite samples: it exhibits a finite probability model, of the product form used for independent repetitions, in which a designated outcome occurs with probability p in (0,1) at every trial while a finite sample avoids it with probability (1-p)^n in (0,1). The item refutes only the implication from a finite sample without the outcome to the falsehood of the declared sampling model; it asserts no experiment, no observed sequence and nothing about the truth or falsity of any physical model.
